notes.meaning: Jacob and his family moved into Egypt to escape a severe famine. Egypt is called the land of Ham because the Egyptians descended from Noah's son Ham through Mizraim. Jacob lived there as an honored guest and a temporary resident, trusting God to watch over them in a foreign land.

God kept His promise to Abraham by causing the Israelites to have many children and grow rapidly. In a relatively short time, they became stronger and more numerous than the Egyptians living around them. Their rapid growth showed that God was actively blessing and protecting His people.

The Egyptian rulers saw how large Israel was becoming and grew fearful and jealous. They turned against God's people, forcing them into harsh slavery and plotting to kill their baby boys. God used even this cruel treatment to prepare His people to leave Egypt and look to Him for rescue.

differ.view: God actively governed the hearts and choices of the Egyptians to fulfill His sovereign plan, while the moral guilt for their wicked hatred belonged entirely to the Egyptians.
God did not put evil hatred into the Egyptians' hearts, but permitted their jealousy to flare up by blessing Israel and removing His restraint.

notes.meaning: God chose Moses and his brother Aaron to lead His people out of bondage. Neither man picked himself for the job; God personally called and equipped them. Moses served as their prophetic leader and governor, while Aaron was chosen to serve as their high priest.

Moses and Aaron performed miracles and spoke God's warnings directly to Pharaoh and his court. These wonders were not just displays of raw power, but unmistakable signs proving that the Lord of Israel is the true God. Each sign warned Egypt that judgment was coming if they continued to defy Him.

God sent a thick, suffocating darkness over the whole land of Egypt as an act of judgment. Even after three days of pitch blackness, Pharaoh and the Egyptians refused to submit to God's command to let His people go. Meanwhile, Moses and Aaron faithfully followed God's instructions without shrinking back.

God struck Egypt's water supplies, turning the great Nile River and all their streams into blood. This wiped out their fish, cutting off both their clean drinking water and a major source of food. It showed that the Lord had complete power over the river that the Egyptians worshiped as a god.

God caused swarms of frogs to come up from the water and cover the entire land. They invaded every private space, including the bedrooms of Pharaoh and his royal officials. Even the king's palace could not keep out the humble creatures God used to bring down Egyptian pride.

God spoke the word, and thick swarms of biting flies and gnats swept across the whole country. These tiny pests caused great irritation and misery from one border of Egypt to the other. The miracle showed that God can use the smallest and most annoying creatures to humble mighty rulers.

Instead of rain, God sent destructive hailstones mixed with flashes of lightning that struck the ground. The storm stripped the vineyards, ruined the fig trees, and shattered timber across the country. This loss wiped out the crops Egypt relied on for food and revealed God's terrifying power over nature.

God commanded massive clouds of locusts to sweep across the land in numbers too large to count. They devoured every green leaf, grass blade, and crop that had survived the hail. This complete ruin left Egypt facing starvation and proved that no earthly ruler can withstand God's command.

God brought the final and most devastating plague by taking the life of every oldest son across Egypt. These firstborn sons represented the pride, strength, and future hope of each family. Because Pharaoh refused to release Israel, whom God called His own firstborn, Egypt suffered the loss of theirs.

God led Israel out of Egypt carrying treasures of silver and gold given to them by their former masters. Remarkably, among the huge crowd leaving, not a single person was weak, sick, or unable to make the journey. God not only repaid them for years of unpaid labor, but also gave them extraordinary physical strength.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern prosperity and healing teachers point to this verse to argue that God guarantees physical health and material wealth to every believer today.

notes.meaning: The Egyptians were glad and relieved when the Israelites finally marched out of the country. The terrifying plagues had filled them with such dread that they feared staying near Israel would mean death for them all. God completely broke the power of the oppressors, making them urge their former slaves to leave.

God gave His people special protection in the wilderness by spreading a massive cloud over them during the day and a pillar of fire at night. The cloud acted like a great tent to shield them from the scorching desert sun. The fire provided light and warmth in the dark, reassuring them of His constant presence.

When the people asked for food, God sent vast flocks of quail into their camp to provide meat. He also fed them daily with manna, which is called the bread of heaven because it fell miraculously from the skies. God showed Himself to be a faithful father who supplies every daily need of His children.

God cracked open a solid rock in the parched desert, and fresh water gushed out in abundance. The water did not merely drip, but flowed through the dry sands like a river to refresh the whole nation. This miracle showed that God can bring life and plenty out of the hardest, most impossible places.

All these wonders took place because God remembered the sacred promise He had made centuries earlier to His servant Abraham. A covenant is God's binding promise, and He will never break His word. Israel was delivered not because they had earned it, but because God is completely faithful to His commitments.

God brought His chosen people out of slavery and into freedom with singing and loud shouts of joy. While Egypt wept over the ruin of its land and people, Israel celebrated God's mighty victory. God delights to replace the long sorrow of His people with joyful praise.

God brought Israel into the land of Canaan and gave them the towns, fields, and vineyards of other nations. The Israelites inherited homes they had not built and ate crops they had not planted. This gift reminded them that the earth belongs to the Lord and that He provides freely for His own.

God gave Israel their freedom and land for a clear purpose: so they would obey His commands and live as His holy people. Deliverance from slavery was meant to lead to thankful, loving obedience to God. The psalm concludes with Hallelujah, which means praise the Lord, inviting everyone to give God the glory He deserves.
